However, dose-related increase in postoperative pain has been seen1 in patients given 25 or 50 mg dihydroco- deine tartrate intravenously after dental surgery, and it has been proposed that dihydrocodeine might act as an antagonist in situ- ations where acute pain was accompanied by high opioid activi- ty.2 Systematic review of the use of single oral doses of dihydroc- odeine has indicated that these are insufficient to provide adequate relief of postoperative pain, and that dihydrocodeine is less effective than ibuprofen.3 1.
